IM11-01.note: Needs GCF*LCM = product of the two numbers; 24n=2160, n=90. Verified unique by search over divisors. No formula supplied. 60 = 360/6 and 144 = 6*24 are real slips; 15 is the thinnest. Nothing reachable without solving.

IM11-02.note: Three-set inclusion-exclusion: 60-27+5=38, 40-38=2. Genuinely at the top of the Upper Level band. 7 is the endpoint of omitting the +5 triple, which is the canonical error. Flag: '5' is a number the stem prints verbatim, so it is a stated quantity on the ballot, but it is a distractor, not the key, so no leak.

IM11-03.note: Add the equations: 8x+8y=72. 72 is the un-divided sum and 36 the halved one; 5 is |x-y| from subtracting instead. Standard 'sum of equations' item, easy for this test.

IM11-04.note: 1#4 = 1-8 = -7; 3#(-7) = 9+14 = 23. 41 is exactly the left-to-right evaluation (3#1)#4 = 7#4 = 41 - a real order-of-operations error, not filler. -5 is the sign flip on the inner result. Defined-operator items are standard ISEE fare; the nesting lifts it to medium.

IM11-05.note: d^2/2 = 50, or side = 10/sqrt(2). No formula printed - the author's claim holds here. But 48 is the endpoint of no error I can construct (side is ~7.07, and 7^2=49, not 48), so one of three distractors is dead. 100 (diagonal read as side) and 200 (d^2 doubled) are fine.

IM11-06.note: 16/144 = 11.1%. 33.3 is the linear ratio 4/12 - the intended trap - and 2.8 is 4/144. FLAG per protocol: 11.1 + 88.9 = 100, a constant the configuration supplies that the stem never prints. It does not hand over the key (a solver must still know which side of the complement is the bull's-eye), but it pairs off two of four options for a guesser and should not be repeated.

IM11-07.note: -27+16 = -11. The three distractors are the three sign/combination errors (-43, 43, 11). Clean, but pure arithmetic - easy.

IM11-08.note: 15 values, 8th in order is 2 (five 0s, two 1s, then the 2s). 0 is the mode and 1.5 is the midpoint of a miscounted list; mean is 1.67, close enough to 1.5 that a mean/median confusion lands near it. Reading a frequency list is a low-difficulty skill here.

IM11-09.note: 3n+2 at n=50. 150 is the off-by-one from 3n, 149 and 147 are the other index slips. The whole item is the off-by-one, which is the right kind of fiddly for this test rather than a reasoning step - medium, not hard.

IM11-10.note: Slope -2, y = -2x+12, x-intercept 6. Note the slope -2 is itself on the ballot as an intermediate you compute on the way - correct distractor design, and it does not aid the key. No line formula supplied.

IM11-11.note: Closing speed 28, 84/28 = 3. Every distractor is 84 divided by the wrong rate (12, 16, 4), which is the complete error family. Easy.

IM11-12.note: 30 = 2(b+8), b = 7. 15 is the brother's age in 8 years - the intermediate, and the trap the item is built around. 11 is 22/2 (the 'twice as old now' misread). Solid age item.

IM11-13.note: 2 x 10^3. Distractors are the exponent slips (200, 18000 from multiplying, 3000). Easy.

IM11-14.note: 6x^3 = 48, x = 2. 8 is 48/6 with the cube root skipped - the exact error the item tests - and 4 and 6 are the other two edges, so a student who solves but answers the wrong edge still lands on a distractor. Volume formula not supplied.

IM11-15.note: r^2 = 162/18 = 9, r = 3. 9 (the intermediate r^2) is the primary trap, 54 is 162/3. Geometric-sequence ratio is on the harder half of Upper Level content but the arithmetic is trivial - medium.

IM11-16.note: Sum 50, median 12, minimize the rest: 1+1+12+12+24. Brute-forced to confirm 24 is the maximum. The binding insight is that the FOURTH value is also >= 12, and 26 is exactly the answer you get if you miss that. 36 is the four-number version. This is the one item in the batch that is hard for the right reason - an extremal constraint, not fiddly arithmetic.

IM11-17.note: D = A + C - B = (3,6). The 'vertices in order' clause is doing real work and the option it exists to exclude, (11,6) = B+C-A (the other parallelogram on the same three points), is ON THE BALLOT - which is what the protocol asks for. Good item.

IM11-18.note: 18 through 90, nine of them; confirmed by enumeration. 8 is the endpoint of dropping 90 (thinking 0 cannot be a digit), which is the intended error; 10 comes from counting 09. Counting item, medium.

IM11-19.note: 12.5 gallons x $3.60 = $45.00. $12.50 is the gallon count dressed as dollars (the intermediate), $100.80 is 28x3.60. Two-step rate item, easy for Upper Level.

IM11-20.note: 686-560 = 126, 126/21 = 6. 46 is total hours worked - the question asks for overtime hours only, and that distinction is the item. 9 = 126/14 (overtime priced at base rate). Every wrong option is a named error.

IM11-21.note: 52 through 148, 25 terms, 25 x 100 = 2500. Verified by enumeration. 2448 drops the first term, 2652 includes 152, 2400 uses 24 terms - all three are endpoint/count errors, the exact failure modes of this item type. 'Between' is unambiguous here since neither 50 nor 150 is a boundary case worth arguing (both are multiples of... 50 is not a multiple of 4; 148 and 152 straddle cleanly). Hard by ISEE standards.

IM11-22.note: -4 - 15 = -19. The 6 p.m. to 11 p.m. interval matches the stated 5 hours, so there is no hidden off-by-one. -15 ignores the starting value, -22 uses 6 hours, 11 flips the sign. Easy.

IM11-23.note: 7 is in the thousandths place. All three distractors are adjacent place values, which is the whole error space. This is an elementary place-value item and sits below the Upper Level band.

IM11-24.note: 18 won, 12 lost, 3:2. '3 to 5' is won-to-total (the standard trap), '2 to 3' is reversed. Easy.

IM11-25.note: 7/3 = 14/6. 42 is 7x6 (multiplying by the denominator twice), 7 is the numerator, 12 is 2x6 ignoring the third. Easy.

IM11-26.note: 10 x 6 = 60; the 8-cm side is a decoy and 80 is its endpoint, 48 pairs the two non-matching numbers, 30 halves it (triangle formula). The configuration is consistent (sin theta = 6/8). RELEVANT TO THE s10 FINDING: the stem does not print A = bh, but it hands you the height explicitly and labels which base it belongs to, so the item tests decoy-resistance, not geometry. It is the closest thing in this batch to the s10 pattern of pre-supplying the ingredient.

IM11-27.note: (2/5)^2. 2/5 is one spin, 4/5 is the sum instead of the product - both are real errors. 1/10 is the weakest of the three; I can only reach it by (2/5)(1/4). Independence is stated plainly, so this is a one-step item.

IM11-28.note: 0.2n = 6. 36 is n+6 (answering the result rather than the number), 5 divides the wrong way, 120 takes 6 as 5 percent. Easy.

IM11-29.note: 5n+10 = S, n = S/5 - 2. S/5 is the MIDDLE term and S/5 + 2 is the GREATEST - so a student who sets it up correctly and then answers the wrong one of the five still lands on a distractor. (S-2)/5 is the misplaced-parenthesis endpoint. Best-designed distractor set in the batch. Algebraic-expression answers push it to medium.

IM11-30.note: 20 boys and 12 girls; 5 + 4 = 9. Both fractions land on integers, so the ratio split is verifiable. 5 and 8 are partial answers (boys only, or 32/4), 23 is the complement. Two chained steps - medium.
